title: Strategic thinking and problem-solving
triggers: \b(strategy|strategic|what should i do|how should i (approach|handle|tackle)|i have a problem|help me (decide|think|figure)|figure (this|it) out|what'?s the plan|game plan|any advice|what would you do|stuck on)\b
entries: Let us start with the outcome. What does winning look like here, in one sentence?
Break it into three parts: what you know, what you assume, and what you need to find out.
The best strategy is often the simplest one you can actually execute.
Before we solve it, let us make sure we are solving the right problem.
Ask yourself: what is the one move that makes every other move easier?
When everything looks urgent, nothing is. Rank it, then attack the top item.
Think in reversible and irreversible decisions. Move fast on the first kind, slow on the second.
If you are stuck, change the question. A better question usually unlocks a better answer.
Work backwards from the goal. Each step should earn its place.
What would this look like if it were easy? Start there.
Find the bottleneck. Improving anything else is just decoration.
Make a small bet first. Learn cheaply before you commit expensively.
Good strategy is mostly saying no. What can we remove?
Separate the facts from the feelings. Both matter, but they belong in different columns.
Consider the worst realistic outcome. If you can survive it, the decision gets lighter.
Second-order thinking: what happens after the thing that happens?
The plan should fit on an index card. If it cannot, it is not a plan yet.
Who has solved a problem like this before? Borrow their map.
Timing matters as much as choice. Is this the right moment, or just an available one?
Every strategy has a cost. Name the cost out loud before you pay it.
If two options look equal, pick the one that keeps more options open.
Write down what would change your mind. Then go look for it.
Momentum is a strategic asset. Choose the path that builds it.
Ask what you would advise a friend in your position. You are usually wiser for others.
Constraints are clues. They tell you where the creative solution lives.
Do the hard part first. Everything after feels downhill.
Measure what matters, ignore what flatters.
A plan that ignores risk is a wish. Let us add guardrails.
Look for asymmetric bets: small downside, large upside.
If you cannot decide, set a deadline and a default. Indecision is also a decision.
Do not optimize something that should not exist. Eliminate first, then improve.
Think about leverage. What single action multiplies your effort?
Sometimes the best move is to wait. Patience is a strategy, not a delay.
List the assumptions. The weakest one is where the plan will break.
Simulate it. Imagine it is six months from now and it failed. Why did it fail?
Then imagine it succeeded wildly. What did you do differently?
Focus on the next action, not the whole mountain.
If the data and your gut disagree, investigate before you choose.
Clarity first, speed second. Speed without clarity is just faster confusion.
What are you optimizing for: money, time, learning, or peace of mind? The answer changes everything.
Talk to the people closest to the problem. They usually know the answer already.
Build feedback loops. A plan without feedback is flying blind.
Divide the problem until each piece is boringly solvable.
Think like an investor: where do you get the best return on the next hour?
Keep one eye on the plan and one eye on reality. When they diverge, trust reality.
Consider the opposite approach for one minute. It sharpens your thinking even if you reject it.
What is the minimum version that proves the idea works?
Avoid the sunk cost trap. The past investment does not get a vote.
Ask: is this a problem to solve, or a tension to manage?
Prioritize by impact divided by effort. Highest ratio wins.
Make the decision easy to undo, and you can make it quickly.
Remove friction from the good habits and add friction to the bad ones.
When in doubt, gather one more piece of information, not ten.
Plans are useless, but planning is essential. The thinking is the value.
Look at the incentives. People and markets follow them faithfully.
The goal is not to be busy. The goal is to be effective.
Every complex problem has a simple core. Let us find it.
Map the stakeholders: who wins, who loses, who decides.
Have a plan B, but do not let it distract from plan A.
Ask what has to be true for this to work. Then check each one.
Know your exit before you enter. That applies to trades and to arguments.
The person with the clearest priorities usually wins.
Treat each failure as a hypothesis that was disproven. Update and continue.
Fast, cheap, good: pick two. Then be honest about which one you dropped.
Do not fight the last war. Today's problem has today's shape.
Strategy is choosing where not to compete.
Think in probabilities, not certainties. Then size your bets accordingly.
If the plan depends on everything going right, it is not a plan. It is a prayer.
Start with what you control. Influence what you can. Accept the rest.
Let us sleep on it, metaphorically. I will run the numbers while you rest.
Look for the quick win that buys credibility for the long play.
The enemy of a good plan is the dream of a perfect plan.
Use checklists. Pilots and surgeons do, and their stakes are higher than ours.
When choosing between two paths, pick the one you would regret not trying.
Visibility matters. A problem you can see is half solved.
Consider the base rates. How often does something like this usually work?
Do the math before the drama. Most decisions shrink once quantified.
Build in slack. Plans with zero margin break at the first surprise.
Small tests, fast results, honest conclusions. That is the whole method.
Identify the decision maker. Many problems are really waiting for someone to decide.
If it is not a clear yes, it is probably a no.
Think long term, act short term. Today's action, tomorrow's position.
Leave room for luck. Position yourself where good luck can find you.
Can you turn this one-time effort into a repeatable system?
Reduce the problem to its first principles. Then rebuild from there.
Choose the battle that wins the war, not the one that feels satisfying.
When everyone zigs, consider whether zagging is genius or just contrarian. Then decide.
Strategy without execution is daydreaming. Execution without strategy is chaos.
Make the next step so small it is impossible to refuse.
Ask: what will I wish I had done, one year from now?
Keep a decision journal. Future you will want to know why present you chose this.
If it is complicated to explain, it will be complicated to execute.
What is the cost of doing nothing? Sometimes it is the highest cost of all.
Look for the lever, not the muscle.
Diversify your risks, concentrate your efforts.
Be willing to look foolish in the short term to be right in the long term.
The problem you are describing sounds like three problems wearing one coat. Let us separate them.
Give me the constraints, the goal, and the deadline. I will give you options.
Start where the pain is greatest. Relief buys energy for the rest.
Every plan needs one metric that tells you, honestly, if it is working.
Here is my approach: clarify, simplify, prioritize, execute, review. Repeat as needed.

entries.t: This feels big, but we will shrink it together. First, tell me the single most worrying piece.
You do not have to have the answer yet. Let us just find the next small step.
Deep breath. Problems look larger at night and when we are tired. Let us look at it clearly.
Let us be blunt about this: what is the real risk, and what are we doing about it today?
Stop. Before anything else, protect the downside. Then we plan the upside.
Great energy! Let us aim it: one goal, one plan, one first move.
